articles.title: The Internet
articles.description: The global network that connects billions of devices.
articles.content:
The internet is a global network of networks that lets billions of devices exchange data using shared rules called protocols, chiefly TCP/IP.

It grew from ARPANET, a US research network that sent its first message in 1969. ARPANET adopted TCP/IP in 1983, and around 1989–1991 Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN, adding pages, links and browsers.

The internet and the web are not the same thing: the internet is the infrastructure of cables, satellites and routers, while the web is one service that runs on it, alongside email, messaging and video calls. More than five billion people use it today.

articles.title: The World Wide Web
articles.description: The linked pages that made the internet easy to browse.
articles.content:
The World Wide Web is a system of linked pages and resources that people access over the internet using a web browser. It was invented by the British scientist Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 while working at CERN, the European physics laboratory, to help researchers share information more easily.

Berners-Lee created the three technologies that still underpin the web: HTML, the language for writing pages; HTTP, the protocol for sending them; and URLs, the addresses that identify each page. The first website went online in 1991. Berners-Lee chose not to patent his invention, making it free for anyone to use, a decision widely credited with helping the web spread so quickly.

Early web browsers such as Mosaic, released in 1993, and Netscape Navigator made the web accessible to ordinary people, and by the mid-1990s it was transforming how people find information, communicate and do business.

articles.title: Computer
articles.description: A machine that processes data by following instructions.
articles.content:
A computer is a machine that follows stored instructions to process data. It takes input, stores and processes information, and produces output.

Early general-purpose electronic machines such as ENIAC (1945) filled entire rooms. The invention of the transistor in 1947 and the integrated circuit in 1958 made computers smaller and cheaper, and the microprocessor in the early 1970s led to personal computers.

Inside a modern computer, the processor (CPU) executes instructions, memory (RAM) holds data in use and storage keeps files. Everything is represented in binary, as ones and zeros.

articles.title: ENIAC
articles.description: One of the first general-purpose electronic computers.
articles.content:
ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, funded by the US Army to calculate artillery firing tables during World War II.

It filled a large room, about 167 square metres, used around 18,000 vacuum tubes, and weighed nearly 30 tonnes. It was reprogrammed by physically rewiring cables and setting switches, a job that could take days, unlike modern computers, which are reprogrammed simply by loading new software.

ENIAC was operated largely by a team of women, including Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings and others, who are now recognised as among the first computer programmers, though their contributions went largely unrecognised for decades. The machine could perform about 5,000 additions per second, extraordinary for its time.

articles.title: The Transistor
articles.description: The tiny switch that built the digital age.
articles.content:
The transistor is a small electronic device that can switch or amplify electrical signals, and it is the basic building block of virtually all modern electronics. It was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs in the United States by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley, who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956.

Transistors replaced older, bulkier and less reliable vacuum tubes, allowing electronic devices to become smaller, cheaper, faster and far more energy-efficient. A single modern computer chip can contain tens of billions of transistors, each only a few nanometres across, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.

Gordon Moore, a co-founder of the chip company Intel, observed in 1965 that the number of transistors on a chip tended to double roughly every two years, a trend known as Moore's Law that has broadly held for decades, though it has slowed as transistors approach the physical limits of how small they can be made.

articles.title: The Microprocessor
articles.description: The computer processor on a single chip.
articles.content:
A microprocessor is a computer's central processing unit built onto a single integrated circuit chip. Before its invention, a computer's processing logic was spread across many separate components, making machines large, expensive and complex to build.

The first commercially available microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was released in 1971. Designed originally for a calculator, it contained about 2,300 transistors, a tiny number compared with the billions found in a modern chip, and could perform roughly 60,000 operations per second.

The microprocessor made possible the personal computer revolution of the late 1970s and 1980s, since it allowed a computer's core processing power to be manufactured cheaply and in large volumes. Today microprocessors are found not only in computers and phones but embedded in cars, appliances and countless other everyday devices.

articles.title: Binary Code
articles.description: The ones and zeros behind every computer.
articles.content:
Binary is a number system that uses only two digits, 0 and 1, unlike the decimal system most people use in daily life, which has ten digits. Computers use binary because their electronic circuits most naturally represent two clear states, such as a switch being off or on, or a voltage being low or high.

Every piece of data a computer stores or processes, whether it is a number, a letter, an image or a piece of music, is ultimately represented as a sequence of binary digits, or bits. Eight bits grouped together form a byte, which can represent 256 different values, enough to encode a single character in many common text encoding systems.

The mathematical foundations of binary logic and computing were laid out by figures including the philosopher and mathematician Gottfried Leibniz in the 17th century and the mathematician George Boole in the 19th century, whose Boolean algebra remains fundamental to how digital logic circuits are designed today.

articles.title: Operating Systems
articles.description: The software that manages a computer's resources.
articles.content:
An operating system is the fundamental software that manages a computer's hardware and resources, providing a common platform on which other application software can run. It handles tasks such as allocating memory, scheduling which programs get access to the processor, and managing files and connected devices such as printers and keyboards.

Early computers in the 1950s and 1960s generally ran one program at a time with no operating system at all, but as computing grew more complex, operating systems developed to allow multiple programs to run seemingly at once and to provide a consistent way for software to interact with varied hardware.

Widely used operating systems today include Microsoft Windows and Apple's macOS for desktop and laptop computers, and Google's Android and Apple's iOS for smartphones, alongside Linux, an open-source operating system first released in 1991 by the Finnish programmer Linus Torvalds, which now powers the majority of the world's web servers and much of the internet's infrastructure.

articles.title: Programming Languages
articles.description: The languages used to instruct computers.
articles.content:
A programming language is a formal language used to write instructions, or code, that a computer can execute. Programmers write in a programming language, which is then translated by software called a compiler or interpreter into the low-level binary instructions that a computer's processor can actually carry out.

Early programming was extremely laborious, often involving directly setting switches or writing in machine code, but the development of higher-level languages such as Fortran in 1957 and COBOL in 1959 made it considerably easier for programmers to write instructions in a form closer to ordinary mathematical notation or English.

Widely used modern languages include Python, valued for being relatively easy to read and learn and now dominant in fields such as data science and artificial intelligence; JavaScript, which runs in nearly every web browser and powers much of the interactivity on websites; and Java and C++, both widely used in large-scale software systems, ranging from banking software to video games.

articles.title: Algorithms
articles.description: Step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.
articles.content:
An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or accomplishing a task, a concept that predates computers by many centuries. The word comes from the Latinised name of the 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose work on systematic methods for solving equations helped lay foundations for algebra itself.

In computing, algorithms are the logical procedures that programs follow to accomplish tasks, ranging from something as simple as sorting a list of numbers into order to something as complex as recommending videos to a user or navigating a self-driving car safely through traffic.

The efficiency of an algorithm, meaning how its speed or memory use grows as the amount of data it processes increases, is a central concern in computer science, since a poorly designed algorithm can become impractically slow on large amounts of data even if it produces a technically correct result, while a well-designed one can handle vast datasets efficiently.

articles.title: Databases
articles.description: Organised systems for storing and retrieving data.
articles.content:
A database is an organised collection of data, structured so that it can be efficiently stored, retrieved, updated and managed, typically through specialised software known as a database management system. Nearly every modern application, from banking systems to social media platforms, relies on databases to keep track of information reliably.

The relational database model, in which data is organised into tables of rows and columns linked by defined relationships, was proposed by the computer scientist Edgar F. Codd in 1970 and remains extremely widely used today, accessed through a standard query language called SQL, developed shortly afterward in the 1970s.

More recently, so-called NoSQL databases have grown in popularity for certain applications, offering more flexible ways of structuring data that can be better suited to handling very large volumes of rapidly changing or loosely structured information, such as that generated by large web applications and social media platforms.

articles.title: Cloud Computing
articles.description: Renting computing power and storage over the internet.
articles.content:
Cloud computing is a model of delivering computing resources, such as processing power, data storage and software, over the internet from remote data centres, rather than requiring individuals or organisations to own and maintain their own physical computer hardware directly.

Instead of buying and running their own servers, businesses and individuals can rent computing capacity from cloud providers as needed, scaling their usage up or down flexibly and typically paying only for the resources they actually consume, an approach that has significantly lowered the barrier to launching new software services and businesses.

Major cloud computing providers include Amazon Web Services, launched in 2006 and widely credited with popularising the modern cloud computing model, along with Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Cloud computing now underpins a vast share of modern internet services, from streaming video platforms to the infrastructure behind many mobile apps.

articles.title: Data Centres
articles.description: The buildings that house the internet's computers.
articles.content:
A data centre is a large, specially designed facility that houses the computer servers, storage systems and networking equipment needed to run internet services, cloud computing platforms and large organisations' computing infrastructure. Modern data centres can contain thousands or even tens of thousands of individual servers operating continuously.

Because servers generate significant heat while running, data centres require extensive cooling systems, and managing this energy use efficiently has become an increasingly important concern as the scale and number of data centres worldwide has grown rapidly, driven partly by the rise of cloud computing and, more recently, by the significant computing demands of training large artificial intelligence models.

Some technology companies have located data centres in naturally cool climates, such as northern Scandinavia, to reduce cooling costs, and have invested heavily in renewable energy to power their operations, reflecting growing attention to the environmental footprint of the digital infrastructure that underpins much of modern life.

articles.title: Cybersecurity
articles.description: Protecting computers, networks and data from attack.
articles.content:
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage and theft.

Common threats include phishing, which uses deceptive messages to steal passwords, malware such as viruses and ransomware, and data breaches. Defences include strong unique passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption, firewalls and regular software updates.

Most attacks succeed by exploiting people rather than technology, so awareness is as important as tools. Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it, and it protects everything from online banking to private messages.

articles.title: Encryption
articles.description: Scrambling information so only the right people can read it.
articles.content:
Encryption is the process of converting readable information, known as plaintext, into a scrambled form called ciphertext, so that it can only be read by someone who possesses the correct key to reverse the process. It has ancient roots, including simple substitution ciphers used by military and political leaders in the classical world.

Modern computing relies heavily on two main types of encryption. Symmetric encryption uses the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data, requiring that key to be shared securely between parties in advance, while asymmetric, or public-key, encryption, developed in the 1970s, uses a mathematically linked pair of keys, one public and one private, allowing secure communication without needing to share a secret key beforehand.

Encryption underpins much of everyday digital life, securing everything from online banking transactions and messaging apps to the padlock icon shown by web browsers when visiting a secure website, and it remains a subject of ongoing debate between privacy advocates and governments concerned about its use by criminals.

articles.title: Malware
articles.description: Software designed to cause harm.
articles.content:
Malware, short for malicious software, is any software specifically designed to damage, disrupt, gain unauthorised access to, or otherwise cause harm to a computer system without the informed consent of its owner. It comes in many different forms, each spreading and operating in distinct ways.

Computer viruses attach themselves to legitimate files or programs and spread when those files are shared or executed, while worms can spread independently across networks without needing a host file at all. Ransomware, which has become an increasingly significant and costly threat in recent years, encrypts a victim's files and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, in exchange for restoring access.

One of the earliest and most famous examples was the Morris Worm, released in 1988, which spread rapidly across the early internet and is widely considered the first major demonstration of how quickly malicious software could spread across a connected network, an early warning of challenges that have grown considerably since.

articles.title: Firewalls
articles.description: The barriers that filter network traffic.
articles.content:
A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules, acting as a barrier between a trusted internal network, such as a home or company network, and untrusted external networks, such as the wider internet.

Early firewalls, developed in the late 1980s, worked primarily by inspecting basic information about data packets, such as their source and destination addresses, to decide whether to allow or block them. Modern firewalls are considerably more sophisticated, often capable of inspecting the actual content of network traffic to detect and block more advanced threats.

Firewalls can be implemented as dedicated hardware devices protecting an entire network, or as software running on an individual computer or server, and they form one layer within a broader approach to network security that also typically includes measures such as encryption, access controls and regular software updates.

articles.title: Passwords
articles.description: The secret words that protect our digital lives.
articles.content:
A password is a secret string of characters used to verify a person's identity and grant access to a computer system, account or device. Despite being one of the oldest and simplest forms of digital security, dating back to some of the earliest shared computer systems in the 1960s, passwords remain the most widely used method of authentication today.

Security experts generally recommend using long, unique passwords for each account, since reusing the same password across multiple services means that a single data breach can expose access to many accounts at once, and many now recommend using a password manager, software that securely generates and stores complex, unique passwords for every account.

Two-factor authentication, which requires a second form of verification alongside a password, such as a code sent to a phone or generated by an app, has become increasingly common as an additional layer of security, since it significantly reduces the risk posed even when a password itself has been stolen or guessed.

articles.title: Hacking
articles.description: Exploring, exploiting and defending computer systems.
articles.content:
Hacking refers to activities that involve identifying and often exploiting weaknesses in computer systems, though the term carries different connotations depending on context and intent. The word originally emerged from a more general engineering and programming culture, particularly around the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the 1950s and 1960s, where it simply meant cleverly and resourcefully solving a technical problem.

Security professionals often distinguish between so-called black-hat hackers, who exploit vulnerabilities for malicious purposes such as theft or disruption, and white-hat, or ethical, hackers, who are often employed or contracted specifically to identify and help fix security weaknesses before malicious actors can exploit them, sometimes through formal bug bounty programmes offered by technology companies.

High-profile hacking incidents, including major data breaches affecting large corporations and even government agencies, have become increasingly common and costly in recent decades, driving significant growth in the cybersecurity industry and increased attention to digital security practices among both organisations and individuals.

articles.title: Open Source Software
articles.description: Software built and shared collaboratively.
articles.content:
Open-source software is software whose underlying source code is made freely available for anyone to view, modify and redistribute, in contrast to proprietary software, where the source code is kept private and controlled exclusively by the company or individual that created it.

The modern open-source movement grew substantially from the 1980s and 1990s onward, with figures such as Richard Stallman, who founded the GNU Project in 1983 to build a free alternative to proprietary operating systems, and Linus Torvalds, whose Linux kernel, first released in 1991, became the foundation for numerous widely used open-source operating systems.

Open-source software now underpins a remarkably large share of modern computing infrastructure, from the servers that run much of the internet to widely used programming tools and web browsers, and it has fostered a distinctive collaborative development model in which volunteers and paid contributors around the world work together, often through platforms such as GitHub, to improve shared codebases over time.

articles.title: Version Control
articles.description: Tracking changes to code and files over time.
articles.content:
Version control is a system for tracking and managing changes made to files, particularly computer code, over time, allowing multiple people to collaborate on the same project while keeping a complete history of every change made, by whom, and why. It has become an essential tool in modern software development.

Before the widespread adoption of formal version control systems, developers often managed changes manually, keeping multiple copies of files with different names, an error-prone approach that made collaboration and tracking down when and why a particular bug was introduced considerably more difficult.

Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to help manage development of the Linux operating system kernel, has become by far the most widely used version control system today, and platforms built around it, particularly GitHub, launched in 2008, have become central hubs for open-source software collaboration and for hosting and sharing code across the software industry.

articles.title: Software Development
articles.description: The process of creating computer programs.
articles.content:
Software development is the overall process of designing, writing, testing and maintaining computer programs, encompassing far more than simply writing code. It typically involves stages including planning and gathering requirements, designing the software's architecture, writing and testing the actual code, and ongoing maintenance after a product has been released.

Various methodologies have been developed to organise this process. The traditional waterfall model, in which each stage is completed fully before moving to the next, has increasingly given way in many organisations to agile methodologies, which emphasise shorter, iterative development cycles, frequent testing and closer, ongoing collaboration with users to adapt to changing requirements throughout a project.

Software bugs, meaning errors or defects in code that cause a program to behave unexpectedly, are a persistent and often costly challenge in development, and rigorous testing practices, including automated testing that can quickly check whether new code changes have broken existing functionality, have become a standard and essential part of professional software development.

articles.title: User Interfaces
articles.description: How people interact with computers.
articles.content:
A user interface is the means by which a person interacts with a computer system or software application, encompassing everything from the visual layout of buttons and menus on a screen to the underlying way commands and information are structured and presented to a user.

Early computers relied almost entirely on command-line interfaces, requiring users to type precise text commands with exact syntax. The graphical user interface, which uses visual elements such as windows, icons and a mouse pointer, was pioneered at Xerox PARC in the 1970s and later popularised commercially by Apple's Macintosh in 1984 and Microsoft Windows shortly afterward, dramatically expanding computing's accessibility to non-technical users.

More recently, touchscreens, popularised by devices such as the iPhone from 2007 onward, and voice interfaces using natural spoken language have introduced further significant shifts in how people interact with computing devices, and designers now place considerable emphasis on usability, meaning how easily and intuitively people can accomplish their goals using a given interface.

articles.title: Emojis
articles.description: Small pictures that add emotion to digital text.
articles.content:
Emojis are small digital images or icons used within text messages and other digital communication to express an emotion, object, or idea, supplementing the words themselves. They were created in Japan in 1999 by Shigetaka Kurita, who designed the first set of 176 emojis for a mobile phone company, drawing inspiration from manga, road signs and Chinese characters.

Emojis remained a largely Japan-specific phenomenon for several years until Unicode, the international standard that assigns unique codes to characters and symbols so they display consistently across different devices and platforms, began incorporating emojis from 2010 onward, allowing them to spread rapidly worldwide as smartphones became common.

New emojis are proposed and formally approved each year by the Unicode Consortium, a process that has occasionally generated public debate over the representation of particular foods, professions, cultures or identities, reflecting the emoji's surprisingly significant role as a form of visual, cross-linguistic digital communication used by billions of people daily.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence
articles.description: Computer systems that perform tasks needing human-like intelligence.
articles.content:
Artificial intelligence is the field of building computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images and making decisions.

The term was coined at a workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956. Modern AI is dominated by machine learning, where systems learn patterns from large amounts of data instead of following hand-written rules. Neural networks with many layers, known as deep learning, drove breakthroughs after 2012 in vision, speech and games.

Large language models, trained on huge collections of text, can write, translate and answer questions. AI also raises questions about accuracy, bias, privacy and the effect on jobs.

articles.title: Machine Learning
articles.description: Systems that learn patterns from data instead of fixed rules.
articles.content:
Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence in which computer systems learn to perform a task by analysing patterns in data, rather than being explicitly programmed with fixed, hand-written rules for every possible situation they might encounter.

In supervised learning, one of the most common approaches, a system is trained on data that has already been labelled with the correct answers, such as thousands of images tagged as containing a cat or not, allowing it to gradually learn to recognise the relevant patterns itself and apply that knowledge to new, unseen examples. Other approaches include unsupervised learning, which looks for patterns in unlabelled data, and reinforcement learning, in which a system learns through trial and error by receiving rewards or penalties for its actions.

Machine learning underpins many everyday technologies, including spam filters that learn to recognise unwanted email, recommendation systems on streaming and shopping platforms, and voice assistants, and its rapid advancement since the 2010s has been driven substantially by the availability of much larger datasets and vastly increased computing power.

articles.title: Neural Networks
articles.description: Computing systems loosely inspired by the brain.
articles.content:
An artificial neural network is a type of computing system loosely inspired by the structure of biological brains, made up of interconnected layers of simple processing units, often called neurons or nodes, that pass signals to one another and adjust the strength of their connections as the network learns.

The basic concept dates back to the 1940s and 1950s, but early neural networks were limited by the modest computing power and small datasets available at the time. Interest surged again from the 2010s onward, particularly following a landmark 2012 result in which a deep neural network dramatically outperformed previous approaches at recognising objects in images, a moment often seen as launching the modern deep learning era.

Deep learning refers to neural networks with many layers stacked between the input and output, allowing them to learn increasingly abstract representations of data. This approach now underlies most cutting-edge AI systems, including image recognition, speech recognition and large language models, though exactly how these networks arrive at particular outputs often remains difficult even for their own creators to fully explain.

articles.title: Large Language Models
articles.description: AI systems trained to understand and generate human language.
articles.content:
A large language model is a type of artificial intelligence system trained on vast amounts of text to predict and generate human-like language, allowing it to answer questions, write text, translate between languages, summarise documents and hold conversations.

These models are built using a neural network architecture called the transformer, introduced by Google researchers in a landmark 2017 paper, which proved particularly effective at processing and generating sequences of text by allowing the model to weigh the relevance of different words to one another across a passage, regardless of their distance apart.

Training a large language model involves exposing it to enormous quantities of text, often drawn from books, websites and other written material, at a computing cost that can run into tens or hundreds of millions of dollars for the largest systems. Since the release of widely publicised chatbots based on these models from 2022 onward, they have been rapidly adopted across many industries, while also raising significant questions about accuracy, bias, copyright and their effect on jobs.

articles.title: Smartphone
articles.description: A pocket computer that also makes phone calls.
articles.content:
A smartphone is a mobile phone that combines calling with a touchscreen computer, a camera, sensors and internet access.

IBM's Simon (1994) is often called the first smartphone, but the category took off after Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007 and Google's Android system followed in 2008. Apps distributed through online stores turned the phone into a platform for maps, banking, games and social media.

A modern smartphone contains a GPS receiver, an accelerometer, a gyroscope and several cameras, and has far more computing power than the computers that guided the Apollo missions. Most of the world's people now own one.

articles.title: Mobile Apps
articles.description: Software built for smartphones and tablets.
articles.content:
A mobile app is a software application designed specifically to run on a smartphone, tablet or other mobile device, typically downloaded and installed through a dedicated digital marketplace known as an app store. The modern app ecosystem began in earnest with Apple's launch of the App Store in 2008, shortly after the release of the original iPhone, followed soon afterward by Google's equivalent store for Android devices.

Apps are generally built in one of two main ways: native apps are developed specifically for a single platform, such as iOS or Android, using tools and programming languages tailored to that system, generally offering the best performance, while cross-platform apps are built using shared code that can run on multiple platforms with less duplicated development effort.

The mobile app economy has grown into a major part of the technology industry, encompassing everything from simple utility apps and games to complex platforms for banking, ride-hailing, food delivery and social media, and app stores typically take a percentage commission on paid app sales and in-app purchases, an arrangement that has drawn increasing regulatory scrutiny in several countries.

articles.title: Social Media
articles.description: Online platforms for sharing and connecting.
articles.content:
Social media refers to websites and applications that allow users to create and share content, and to build networks of connections with other people, typically organised around personal profiles, posts and various forms of interaction such as comments, likes and shares.

Early social networking sites such as Friendster, launched in 2002, and MySpace, which followed shortly after, demonstrated the appeal of online social networking, but Facebook, founded by Mark Zuckerberg and fellow Harvard students in 2004 and opened to the general public in 2006, grew to become the dominant platform of its era, eventually reaching billions of users worldwide.

Subsequent platforms, including Twitter, launched in 2006 and later rebranded as X, Instagram, founded in 2010, and TikTok, which achieved explosive global growth internationally from around 2018 onward, have each introduced distinctive formats, from short text posts to photo sharing and short-form video, shaping how billions of people communicate, consume news and entertainment, and present themselves online.

articles.title: Search Engines
articles.description: The tools that help us find information online.
articles.content:
A search engine is a software system designed to search for information across the vast, ever-growing collection of pages that make up the World Wide Web, returning a ranked list of results based on their relevance to a user's typed query. Early web search engines in the mid-1990s, including AltaVista and Yahoo, relied largely on simpler methods of indexing and matching keywords.

Google, founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin while they were graduate students at Stanford University, introduced an influential ranking algorithm called PageRank, which judged a page's importance partly by how many other pages linked to it, an approach that produced noticeably more relevant results than earlier competitors and helped Google rapidly become the dominant search engine worldwide.

Modern search engines use vastly more sophisticated methods, including machine learning techniques that attempt to understand the underlying intent behind a search query rather than simply matching keywords, and they continuously update their vast indexes of web pages to keep pace with the constantly changing content of the internet.

articles.title: Email
articles.description: Electronic mail, one of the internet's original services.
articles.content:
Email, short for electronic mail, is a method of exchanging digital messages between people over a computer network, and it remains one of the oldest and most enduringly important services on the internet. The first email sent between separate computers on a network is generally credited to the American computer engineer Ray Tomlinson in 1971, who is also credited with popularising the use of the @ symbol to separate a username from the computer, or later domain, it belonged to.

Email adoption grew substantially through the 1980s and 1990s as computer networks expanded and became more interconnected, eventually becoming a standard tool for both personal and, especially, professional and business communication worldwide, largely displacing traditional postal mail for many everyday communication purposes.

Despite the later rise of instant messaging and social media, email has remained essential for formal communication, account registration and verification, and many workplace communications, though it also faces ongoing challenges from unwanted spam messages and increasingly sophisticated phishing scams designed to trick recipients into revealing sensitive information.

articles.title: Instant Messaging
articles.description: Real-time text conversation over the internet.
articles.content:
Instant messaging refers to real-time text-based communication between users over the internet, distinguished from email primarily by its immediacy, since messages are typically delivered and can be responded to within seconds rather than being checked periodically like a traditional inbox.

Early instant messaging services such as ICQ, launched in 1996, and subsequently AOL Instant Messenger, popularised the format for personal use during the late 1990s and early 2000s, primarily on desktop computers. The rise of smartphones brought a new generation of mobile-first messaging apps, including WhatsApp, launched in 2009 and later acquired by Facebook, which introduced widespread use of end-to-end encryption to protect the privacy of conversations.

Modern messaging apps have expanded considerably beyond simple text, now commonly supporting voice and video calls, file and photo sharing, group conversations and, in some cases, payments, and they have become central to both personal communication and, in many countries and industries, business and customer service interactions.

articles.title: Video Streaming
articles.description: Watching video content delivered over the internet.
articles.content:
Video streaming is the delivery of video content over the internet in a continuous flow, allowing viewers to begin watching almost immediately rather than needing to download an entire file first. Early online video was limited by slow internet connections and small, low-quality video windows, but improvements in internet speed and video compression technology gradually made higher-quality streaming practical.

YouTube, founded in 2005 and acquired by Google the following year, pioneered mainstream user-generated video sharing, allowing anyone to upload and share video content freely. Subscription streaming services for professionally produced film and television content, led particularly by Netflix, which pivoted from mailing DVDs to offering internet streaming from 2007 onward, subsequently transformed how many people watch television and film, contributing to a significant decline in traditional broadcast television viewership in many countries.

The streaming model has since expanded to music, with services such as Spotify, launched in 2008, and to live video, including video game streaming platforms such as Twitch, reflecting a broader shift across the media industry away from owning physical or downloaded copies of content toward accessing it on demand.

articles.title: Wi-Fi
articles.description: The wireless technology that connects our devices.
articles.content:
Wi-Fi is a wireless networking technology that allows electronic devices such as computers, smartphones and smart home devices to connect to the internet and to each other without physical cables, using radio waves to transmit data over relatively short distances, typically covering a home, office or public space.

The technology was formally standardised in 1997 under a set of technical specifications known as IEEE 802.11, and the Wi-Fi Alliance, an industry group formed in 1999, subsequently developed the Wi-Fi brand name specifically to make the technology easier for consumers to recognise and trust across different manufacturers' devices, since the original technical standard name was considered too cumbersome for everyday marketing use.

Wi-Fi has become essential infrastructure in homes, offices, schools and countless public spaces such as cafés and airports worldwide, and successive generations of the technology have delivered substantially faster speeds and improved the ability to handle many simultaneously connected devices, an increasingly important capability as the number of internet-connected devices in a typical household continues to grow.

articles.title: Bluetooth
articles.description: Short-range wireless connections between devices.
articles.content:
Bluetooth is a wireless technology standard used for exchanging data over short distances, typically no more than about ten metres, between fixed and mobile devices, commonly used to connect devices such as wireless headphones, keyboards, speakers and fitness trackers to a phone or computer without physical cables.

The technology was developed in the 1990s by the Swedish telecommunications company Ericsson and is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Scandinavian king credited with uniting rival tribes in Denmark, a historical reference chosen to reflect the technology's original goal of uniting different competing wireless communication standards under one common system.

Bluetooth has become especially prominent through wireless earbuds and headphones, and low-energy versions of the technology, introduced from around 2010 onward, have made it practical to use in small battery-powered devices such as fitness trackers and smart home sensors that need to operate for extended periods, sometimes months or years, without needing a battery recharge.

articles.title: GPS
articles.description: The satellite system that tells us where we are.
articles.content:
GPS, the Global Positioning System, is a satellite-based navigation system that allows a receiver, such as one built into a smartphone or car, to determine its precise location anywhere on Earth by receiving and processing signals from multiple orbiting satellites simultaneously.

The system was developed by the United States military, with its first satellite launched in 1978, and was originally restricted primarily to military use before being made available for civilian applications, with full accuracy for civilian users only becoming available in the year 2000, when a deliberate degradation of the signal for non-military users was switched off.

A GPS receiver calculates its position by precisely measuring the time it takes for signals to arrive from at least four different satellites simultaneously, since knowing the small differences in arrival times allows the receiver to calculate its distance from each satellite and thereby triangulate its own exact position. GPS now underpins navigation apps, ride-hailing services, precision agriculture and countless other applications well beyond its original military purpose.

articles.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
articles.description: Immersive and blended digital experiences.
articles.content:
Virtual reality, or VR, refers to technology that creates a fully immersive, computer-generated environment that a user experiences through a headset, replacing their view of the physical world entirely with a simulated one. Augmented reality, by contrast, overlays digital information or images onto a user's view of the real world, typically through a phone screen or transparent headset display, rather than replacing it.

Early experimental VR systems date back to the 1960s, but the technology remained largely confined to research labs, flight simulators and niche applications for decades due to the high cost and limited capability of the necessary hardware. Renewed mainstream interest developed considerably from the 2010s onward, driven by improvements in display technology, motion tracking and computing power, alongside major investment from large technology companies.

Applications for VR and AR now range from video gaming and immersive entertainment to professional training simulations, such as for surgery or industrial equipment operation, and architectural and design visualisation, though widespread everyday consumer adoption has developed more gradually than some early predictions suggested.

articles.title: Quantum Computing
articles.description: Computing that exploits the strange rules of quantum physics.
articles.content:
Quantum computing is an emerging approach to computation that exploits principles from quantum mechanics, the branch of physics describing the behaviour of matter at extremely small scales, to potentially perform certain specific types of calculations far faster than even the most powerful conventional computers.

Unlike a classical computer bit, which must be either a 0 or a 1, a quantum bit, or qubit, can exist in a combination of both states simultaneously, a phenomenon known as superposition, and qubits can also become linked together through a property called entanglement, allowing quantum computers to explore many possible solutions to certain problems in parallel in ways that classical computers cannot easily replicate.

Quantum computers remain at a relatively early experimental stage of development, requiring extremely challenging engineering conditions such as temperatures colder than outer space to keep the fragile qubits stable enough to function reliably. Researchers believe the technology could eventually prove particularly valuable for specific applications such as simulating complex molecules for drug discovery and certain types of cryptography and optimisation problems, though building large-scale, reliable quantum computers remains a substantial ongoing technical challenge.

articles.title: Robotics
articles.description: The science of designing and building robots.
articles.content:
Robotics is the field that designs, builds and programs robots, which are machines that sense their surroundings and act on them.

A robot typically combines sensors, a controller and actuators such as motors. The first industrial robot, Unimate, began work on a General Motors assembly line in 1961. Today robots weld cars, assemble electronics, explore Mars, assist in surgery and vacuum floors.

The word robot comes from the Czech word robota, meaning forced labour, and was popularised by Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. Modern research focuses on robots that can learn, walk on legs and work safely beside people.

articles.title: 3D Printing
articles.description: Building physical objects layer by layer.
articles.content:
3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, is a process for creating three-dimensional physical objects by building them up gradually, layer by layer, from a digital design file, in contrast to traditional manufacturing methods that typically involve cutting, drilling or moulding material away from or into a larger block.

The technology's origins trace to the 1980s, when the American engineer Chuck Hull invented a process called stereolithography in 1983, using a laser to solidify liquid resin layer by layer to build up solid objects, and subsequently founded a company to commercialise the technology, helping to establish the foundations of the modern 3D printing industry.

3D printing is now used across a wide range of applications, from rapid prototyping in product design and engineering, to manufacturing customised medical devices such as prosthetics and dental implants tailored precisely to an individual patient, to producing complex aerospace components that would be difficult or impossible to manufacture using traditional methods, and increasingly by hobbyists using relatively affordable desktop 3D printers at home.

articles.title: Drones
articles.description: Unmanned aircraft with many civilian and military uses.
articles.content:
A drone, formally known as an unmanned aerial vehicle, is an aircraft that operates without a human pilot physically on board, instead being controlled remotely by a human operator or, increasingly, flying with significant autonomous capability guided by onboard computer systems and sensors.

Military use of unmanned aircraft dates back for decades, but consumer and commercial drone technology expanded rapidly from around the 2010s onward, driven substantially by improvements in lightweight batteries, miniaturised cameras and increasingly affordable GPS and stabilisation systems that made small, relatively low-cost drones practical for a wide range of civilian uses.

Today drones are used for purposes including aerial photography and filmmaking, agricultural monitoring of crops, package delivery trials by several major companies, search and rescue operations, and building inspection, alongside their continued and often controversial military applications, and their growing prevalence has prompted many countries to introduce specific aviation regulations governing where and how drones can be legally flown.

articles.title: Wearable Technology
articles.description: Computers you can wear on your body.
articles.content:
Wearable technology refers to electronic devices designed to be worn on the body, typically incorporating sensors and computing capability to monitor aspects of the wearer's activity, health or environment, often while remaining discreet or fashionable enough for regular everyday use.

Early digital wearables such as calculator watches appeared as novelty consumer products from the late 1970s and 1980s, but the modern wearable technology category expanded substantially with the introduction of fitness trackers, such as those popularised by the company Fitbit from around 2009 onward, and subsequently with smartwatches, notably including the Apple Watch, launched in 2015, which combined fitness tracking with broader smartphone-like functionality.

Modern wearable devices commonly track metrics such as heart rate, sleep patterns, step counts and, in more advanced models, blood oxygen levels and even early indicators of certain heart conditions, and the substantial health-related data they collect has prompted growing interest from both individual users seeking personal health insights and researchers studying population-level health and fitness trends at scale.

articles.title: E-commerce
articles.description: Buying and selling online.
articles.content:
E-commerce, short for electronic commerce, refers to the buying and selling of goods and services conducted over the internet, encompassing everything from large online retail marketplaces to small individual businesses selling directly through their own websites or social media pages.

Amazon, founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994 initially as an online bookstore, grew over subsequent decades into one of the world's largest and most influential e-commerce companies, expanding into nearly every category of retail goods and pioneering practices such as extensive customer reviews and highly efficient, fast delivery logistics that reshaped consumer expectations across the wider retail industry.

E-commerce has continued to grow rapidly worldwide, accelerated notably by a significant surge in online shopping during the COVID-19 pandemic beginning in 2020, and it has substantially reshaped the traditional retail industry, contributing to considerable change and closures among physical brick-and-mortar stores in many countries while also creating entirely new opportunities for small businesses and independent sellers to reach global customers directly online.

articles.title: The History of Computing
articles.description: From mechanical calculators to modern machines.
articles.content:
The history of computing spans from early mechanical calculating devices to today's powerful digital machines. In the early 19th century the English mathematician Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer that was never fully built in his lifetime but is now regarded as containing many of the essential concepts of modern computing.

Working alongside Babbage, the mathematician Ada Lovelace wrote what is widely considered the first computer program, a detailed method for the Analytical Engine to calculate a particular mathematical sequence, along with remarkably prescient notes suggesting that such a machine could one day be used for far more than pure calculation, including composing music.

The first fully electronic general-purpose computers appeared in the 1940s during and shortly after World War II, and computing has since progressed through several distinct eras, from room-sized mainframe computers used mainly by large organisations, to smaller minicomputers, to the personal computer revolution of the late 1970s and 1980s, and finally to today's smartphones, which carry vastly more computing power in a pocket than the room-sized machines of only a few decades ago.

articles.title: Charles Babbage
articles.description: The Victorian inventor of the first mechanical computer designs.
articles.content:
Charles Babbage (1791–1871) was an English mathematician, philosopher and mechanical engineer, widely regarded as the father of the computer for his pioneering, though ultimately unfinished, designs for mechanical general-purpose computing machines during the early to mid-19th century.

His first major design, the Difference Engine, was intended to automatically calculate mathematical tables, which at the time were laboriously and error-pronely calculated and printed by hand, a process highly vulnerable to human mistakes with potentially serious consequences in fields such as navigation and engineering that relied on their accuracy. His later, far more ambitious design, the Analytical Engine, conceived from 1837 onward, included concepts remarkably similar to those found in modern computers, including a form of memory and the ability to be programmed using punched cards.

Babbage never completed a full working version of either machine during his lifetime, partly due to the immense mechanical engineering precision they required, which exceeded what contemporary manufacturing technology could reliably achieve, and partly due to funding difficulties. A complete working Difference Engine was finally built from his original detailed designs in 1991, using period-appropriate manufacturing techniques, and successfully demonstrated that his designs would indeed have worked.

articles.title: Ada Lovelace
articles.description: The mathematician often called the first computer programmer.
articles.content:
Ada Lovelace (1815–1852), born Augusta Ada Byron and the only legitimate daughter of the poet Lord Byron, was an English mathematician best known for her detailed work on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, an unbuilt mechanical general-purpose computer designed during the early to mid-19th century.

In 1843 she published an extensive set of translated notes on the Analytical Engine, considerably longer than the original French article she had been translating, which included what is now widely regarded as the first published algorithm specifically intended to be carried out by a machine, a detailed method for calculating a sequence of numbers known as Bernoulli numbers.

Beyond the specific algorithm itself, Lovelace's notes showed a remarkably prescient understanding that such a machine could potentially manipulate not just numbers but any information that could be represented symbolically, including music and images, a conceptual leap toward the modern idea of a general-purpose computer that went considerably further than Babbage's own more narrowly numerical focus. The programming language Ada, developed for the US Department of Defense in the early 1980s, was later named in her honour.

articles.title: Alan Turing
articles.description: The mathematician who laid the theoretical foundations of computing.
articles.content:
Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician, logician and codebreaker widely regarded as one of the founding figures of modern computer science and artificial intelligence. In a landmark 1936 paper, he introduced the concept of what is now called a Turing machine, a simple theoretical device that formally captured the essential nature of computation and helped establish the theoretical limits of what any computer could ever calculate.

During World War II, Turing worked at Bletchley Park in England as part of a team that successfully broke the German Enigma cipher, used to encrypt military communications, and his contributions to codebreaking are widely credited with significantly shortening the war and saving many lives, work that remained officially classified for decades after the war ended.

In 1950 Turing proposed what became known as the Turing Test, a way of assessing whether a machine's conversational responses could be indistinguishable from those of a human, a concept that remains influential in discussions of artificial intelligence today. Turing was prosecuted in 1952 under then-existing British laws criminalising homosexuality and died in 1954; he received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013, and the UK government has since apologised for his historical treatment.

articles.title: John von Neumann
articles.description: The mathematician behind the modern computer's basic design.
articles.content:
John von Neumann (1903–1957) was a Hungarian-American mathematician and physicist who made foundational contributions across an unusually broad range of fields, including pure mathematics, quantum physics, economics and, notably, the fundamental architecture underlying nearly all modern computers.

In 1945 he authored an influential report describing what became known as the von Neumann architecture, in which a computer stores both its program instructions and the data it operates on together in the same memory, an elegantly simple design that remains the basic conceptual model underlying the overwhelming majority of computers built since, from early room-sized machines to today's smartphones.

Von Neumann also made major contributions to game theory, an important branch of mathematics later widely applied in economics, and worked as a senior scientist on the Manhattan Project, the wartime programme that developed the first nuclear weapons. He was renowned among his contemporaries for an exceptional breadth of expertise and an unusually rapid, intuitive grasp of highly complex problems across strikingly diverse fields.

articles.title: Grace Hopper
articles.description: The programming pioneer who made computers speak English.
articles.content:
Grace Hopper (1906–1992) was an American computer scientist and United States Navy rear admiral who made pioneering contributions to programming language development, particularly in helping make computer programming considerably more accessible by moving away from complex, numerically based machine code.

In 1952 she developed one of the first compilers, a type of software that translates human-written, more English-like programming instructions into the low-level machine code a computer's processor can actually execute, a foundational innovation for higher-level programming. She subsequently played a significant leading role in the development of COBOL, a programming language released in 1959 and specifically designed for business applications, using more readable, English-like syntax, which remained widely used in many large financial and government computer systems for decades afterward.

Hopper is also widely, though somewhat apocryphally, credited with popularising the term computer bug, after an incident in 1947 in which a real moth was found causing a malfunction inside an early computer relay, and the insect was subsequently taped into a technical logbook as a memento. She continued an active and influential career in computing and naval service well into her seventies.

articles.title: Tim Berners-Lee
articles.description: The inventor of the World Wide Web.
articles.content:
Tim Berners-Lee, born in London in 1955, is a British computer scientist credited with inventing the World Wide Web in 1989 while working as a researcher at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory near Geneva, where he was seeking a more efficient way for the laboratory's many international researchers to share and link documents and data.

He developed the three core technologies that remain foundational to how the web works today: HTML, the markup language used to structure and format web pages; HTTP, the protocol computers use to request and transmit those pages over a network; and the URL, the standardised addressing system that identifies the specific location of any given page or resource.

Notably, Berners-Lee made a deliberate decision not to patent his invention or attempt to profit exclusively from it, choosing instead to make the underlying technology freely available to everyone, a decision widely credited as instrumental in allowing the web to be adopted and to grow so rapidly and openly worldwide. He was knighted in 2004 for his contributions and has continued to be an influential advocate for an open, decentralised internet, including through later efforts aimed at giving users greater control over their personal data.

articles.title: Bill Gates
articles.description: The Microsoft co-founder who helped popularise personal computing.
articles.content:
Bill Gates, born in the United States in 1955, co-founded the software company Microsoft together with his childhood friend Paul Allen in 1975, and led the company as it grew to become the dominant force in personal computer software throughout the 1980s and 1990s, playing a central role in bringing computing into homes and offices worldwide.

Microsoft's MS-DOS operating system, and subsequently its Windows graphical operating system, first released in 1985, became the standard software running on the vast majority of personal computers sold globally for decades, a dominant market position that made Gates for a period the wealthiest person in the world and made Microsoft one of the most valuable and influential technology companies ever created.

Gates stepped back from his day-to-day leadership role at Microsoft in the early 2000s to focus increasingly on philanthropy, co-founding the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, which has become one of the largest and most influential charitable foundations in the world, directing very substantial funding toward global health initiatives, including vaccine development and distribution, and toward education reform efforts, particularly in the United States.

articles.title: Steve Jobs
articles.description: The Apple co-founder known for transformative product design.
articles.content:
Steve Jobs (1955–2011) co-founded the technology company Apple together with Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne in 1976, and became renowned over his career for his distinctive, exacting focus on product design and user experience, helping to establish Apple's particular reputation for elegantly designed, carefully considered consumer technology products.

After being controversially removed from Apple's leadership in 1985 following internal boardroom disputes, Jobs founded a new computer company, NeXT, and separately acquired and led the computer animation studio Pixar, which went on to produce a series of critically and commercially successful animated films, before eventually returning to lead Apple again in 1997, at a time when the company was struggling significantly and facing serious financial difficulties.

Under his renewed leadership, Apple launched a remarkable series of highly influential products, including the iMac in 1998, the iPod in 2001, which considerably reshaped the music industry, the iPhone in 2007, which redefined the smartphone category and much of the wider technology industry that followed it, and the iPad in 2010. Jobs died in 2011 from complications related to pancreatic cancer, and he remains widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the history of consumer technology and product design.

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg
articles.description: The Facebook founder who built a global social network.
articles.content:
Mark Zuckerberg, born in the United States in 1984, founded the social networking service Facebook in 2004 while a student at Harvard University, initially launching it as a platform restricted to Harvard students before gradually expanding access to other universities and eventually opening it to the general public worldwide in 2006.

Under his continued leadership, Facebook grew rapidly to become one of the largest and most influential technology companies in the world, eventually reaching billions of active users globally, and the company subsequently expanded its reach considerably further by acquiring other major platforms, including the photo-sharing app Instagram in 2012 and the messaging service WhatsApp in 2014.

In 2021 the parent company was renamed Meta, reflecting a significant strategic shift in focus toward developing what Zuckerberg described as the metaverse, a proposed set of immersive, interconnected virtual environments accessed particularly through virtual and augmented reality technology. Zuckerberg and his company have faced substantial and sustained public and regulatory scrutiny over the years regarding issues including user data privacy, the spread of misinformation on the platform, and the broader societal and psychological effects of widespread social media use.

articles.title: Apple
articles.description: The technology company behind the Mac, iPhone and iPad.
articles.content:
Apple is an American technology company founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, initially to sell a personal computer kit that Wozniak had largely designed himself. The company's early Apple II computer, released in 1977, became one of the first widely successful mass-market personal computers, helping to establish the young personal computer industry more broadly.

After a period of internal difficulty in the mid-1980s that saw Jobs depart the company, Apple's fortunes were dramatically transformed following his return in 1997, with a subsequent series of highly influential product launches, including the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad, that collectively repositioned Apple as one of the world's most valuable and closely watched technology companies, known for tightly integrating its hardware and software design.

Apple has continued to expand well beyond its original computer hardware business into areas including digital services, such as its App Store and streaming offerings, and wearable devices such as the Apple Watch and AirPods wireless earbuds, and the company has become known for a distinctive, closely controlled ecosystem approach in which its various hardware and software products are specifically designed to work together closely.

articles.title: Google
articles.description: The company behind the world's dominant search engine.
articles.content:
Google is an American technology company founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, two graduate students at Stanford University, who developed an influential search ranking algorithm called PageRank that helped the company's search engine quickly become widely regarded as considerably more useful and relevant than its early competitors.

Beyond its core search engine, which remains a dominant global product used by billions of people, Google has expanded very substantially over the years into numerous other significant areas, including the Android mobile operating system, acquired in 2005 and now running on the large majority of the world's smartphones, the Chrome web browser, the video platform YouTube, acquired in 2006, and a wide range of cloud computing and productivity software services used by both individuals and businesses.

In 2015 Google reorganised its various business activities under a new parent holding company called Alphabet, a structural change intended to separate its core, highly profitable advertising and search business more clearly from other, often more experimental and longer-term ventures, including autonomous vehicle development through its Waymo subsidiary and various other ambitious research projects.

articles.title: Amazon
articles.description: The e-commerce giant that expanded into cloud computing.
articles.content:
Amazon is an American e-commerce and technology company founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994, initially launched as an online bookstore operating out of a rented garage, before rapidly expanding to sell an enormously wide range of other product categories over the following years, eventually growing into one of the largest and most diversified retailers in the world.

The company has become particularly known for its highly efficient logistics and delivery operations, built around a vast global network of warehouses, known within the company as fulfilment centres, and its Prime subscription service, launched in 2005, which offers fast, often next-day shipping alongside a range of other bundled services including video and music streaming.

Beyond retail, Amazon Web Services, its cloud computing division launched in 2006, has grown to become one of the most significant and profitable parts of the overall company, providing the underlying computing infrastructure that powers a very large share of major websites and online applications and services used worldwide, from small startups to major corporations and government agencies.

articles.title: The Microchip
articles.description: The integrated circuit that shrank electronics.
articles.content:
A microchip, or integrated circuit, is a small piece of semiconductor material, almost always silicon, onto which a complete electronic circuit, potentially containing billions of individual transistors and other electronic components, is fabricated as a single compact unit, dramatically reducing the size, cost and power consumption of electronic devices compared with using separate individual components wired together.

The integrated circuit was invented independently and almost simultaneously in the late 1950s by two American engineers, Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor, both of whom recognised that multiple electronic components could be manufactured together on a single piece of semiconductor material rather than being built and wired together separately, a breakthrough insight that fundamentally transformed the entire electronics industry.

Modern microchip manufacturing is an extraordinarily precise and complex process, carried out in specialised facilities called fabrication plants, or fabs, that require an exceptionally clean, controlled environment, since even microscopic dust particles can ruin the incredibly small circuit patterns, some now measured in mere nanometres, etched onto each chip using advanced techniques such as photolithography.

articles.title: The Semiconductor Industry
articles.description: The global business of making computer chips.
articles.content:
The semiconductor industry designs and manufactures the computer chips that power virtually all modern electronic devices, from smartphones and cars to household appliances and advanced military equipment, and it has grown into one of the most technologically sophisticated and strategically significant manufacturing industries in the world.

Chip manufacturing has become highly specialised and geographically concentrated, with a small handful of companies possessing the extraordinarily expensive, cutting-edge manufacturing capability required to produce the most advanced chips. Taiwan's TSMC, founded in 1987, has become particularly dominant in this most advanced segment of chip manufacturing, producing chips for numerous major global technology companies that themselves design chips but do not operate their own advanced manufacturing facilities.

Because of the industry's critical importance to modern economies, national security applications and the broader technology sector, and its notably concentrated global supply chain, semiconductor manufacturing has increasingly become a significant focus of government policy and international trade tensions in recent years, with several major countries investing substantial public funding specifically to encourage more domestic chip manufacturing capacity within their own borders.

articles.title: Barcodes
articles.description: The stripes that let machines read product information.
articles.content:
A barcode is a machine-readable pattern, typically consisting of a series of parallel black and white lines or, more recently, a two-dimensional pattern such as a QR code, that encodes information which can be quickly and accurately scanned and read by an optical scanning device, considerably speeding up and improving the accuracy of processes such as retail checkout and inventory tracking.

The first practical commercial barcode system was demonstrated in 1974, when a scanner successfully read a barcode on a pack of chewing gum at a supermarket checkout in Ohio, an item now preserved in the Smithsonian Institution, marking a significant early milestone in the widespread commercial adoption of barcode technology across the retail industry.

QR codes, a two-dimensional form of barcode capable of storing considerably more information than a traditional linear barcode, were originally developed in Japan in 1994 for tracking automotive parts during vehicle manufacturing, but they have since become extremely widely used for purposes including making mobile payments, sharing website links quickly, and displaying restaurant menus, particularly following a substantial surge in their everyday use during the COVID-19 pandemic.

articles.title: Digital Photography
articles.description: How cameras moved from film to sensors.
articles.content:
Digital photography captures and stores images electronically using a digital image sensor, rather than exposing and developing light-sensitive chemical film, as was standard practice throughout most of photography's earlier history before the technology's widespread digital transition from the 1990s onward.

The first working digital camera prototype was built in 1975 by the American electrical engineer Steven Sasson while working at Kodak, though it was a bulky, relatively low-resolution device that took nearly 23 seconds simply to record a single black-and-white image to cassette tape, and the technology remained largely experimental for many years afterward before gradually becoming commercially practical.

Digital photography became increasingly mainstream and broadly accessible to ordinary consumers through the late 1990s and 2000s, and it was subsequently transformed even further by the near-universal integration of increasingly capable digital cameras directly into smartphones from the late 2000s onward, a shift that has made photography an extremely common, immediate and widely shared everyday activity for billions of people worldwide, fundamentally changing how people document and share their daily lives.

articles.title: Digital and Cryptocurrency
articles.description: Money that exists only in electronic form.
articles.content:
Digital currency refers broadly to any form of money that exists only in electronic form, without a physical equivalent such as printed banknotes or minted coins, a category that includes both currency issued and controlled by traditional central banks and financial institutions, and newer decentralised cryptocurrencies not controlled by any single central authority.

Bitcoin, introduced in 2008 through a paper published under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto and launched as a working network in January 2009, was the first major cryptocurrency, and it introduced blockchain technology, a distributed, cryptographically secured public ledger that records every transaction across a decentralised network of computers, without needing a central bank or other single trusted authority to verify and process the transactions.

Since Bitcoin's launch, thousands of alternative cryptocurrencies have been created, and the technology has attracted both enthusiastic supporters, who emphasise its decentralised, censorship-resistant nature, and significant criticism, particularly regarding the very large amounts of energy required by some cryptocurrency networks, the substantial price volatility many cryptocurrencies have historically exhibited, and their notable use in various illicit activities, prompting a wide range of differing regulatory responses across different countries worldwide.

articles.title: Electric Cars
articles.description: Vehicles driven by batteries and electric motors.
articles.content:
An electric car is powered by an electric motor and a rechargeable battery instead of a petrol or diesel engine. Electric cars were built as early as the 1830s and were common around 1900, but were pushed aside by cheap petrol cars.

They returned in the 2000s thanks to lithium-ion batteries, improving range and concern about emissions. Tesla's Roadster (2008) and later mass-market models helped make them mainstream, and by the 2020s nearly every major carmaker offered electric models.

They produce no exhaust at the tailpipe and are very efficient, and regenerative braking recovers energy when slowing down. Their overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated and on battery manufacturing and recycling, and charging infrastructure remains a challenge in many countries.

articles.title: Computer Programming
articles.description: Writing instructions that tell a computer what to do.
articles.content:
Computer programming is the process of writing instructions, called code, that tell a computer what to do, using a programming language. Code is translated by a compiler or interpreter into instructions the machine can run.

Programs are built from basic building blocks such as variables, which store data, conditions, which allow different outcomes depending on circumstances, loops, which repeat actions, and functions, which group instructions that can be reused. Larger software projects are organised into modules and libraries so that different parts of a program, and often different teams of programmers, can work together.

Learning to program has become increasingly accessible through free online courses and resources, and it is now taught in many schools worldwide as a foundational skill, reflecting how central software has become to modern life, from the apps on a phone to the systems that run hospitals, banks and factories.

articles.title: Blockchain
articles.description: A shared ledger of linked, tamper-resistant records.
articles.content:
A blockchain is a shared digital ledger that records transactions in linked blocks, so that no single party controls the record. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, so changing an old entry would break every later link and be noticed.

Many computers keep copies of the ledger and agree on new blocks through a consensus method such as proof of work or proof of stake. Bitcoin, described in 2008 by the person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto and launched in 2009, was the first major blockchain application.

The technology is also used for other cryptocurrencies, smart contracts, which automatically execute agreements when conditions are met, and supply-chain tracking, though it can consume a lot of energy, particularly under proof of work, and does not suit every problem despite considerable hype about its potential uses.

articles.title: 5G
articles.description: The fifth generation of mobile networks.
articles.content:
5G is the fifth generation of mobile network technology, following 4G LTE, designed for higher speeds, lower delay and more connected devices.
