It uses a wider range of radio frequencies, including high-frequency millimetre-wave bands that carry huge amounts of data over short distances, and it relies on many small cells.

In ideal conditions download speeds can reach several gigabits per second, and latency can fall to a few milliseconds, fast enough to enable applications that were impractical with earlier network generations. Commercial 5G networks began launching in 2019, and adoption has since spread across much of the world.

Besides faster phones, 5G is meant to support connected factories, remote surgery, smart cities and large numbers of internet-of-things sensors, though realising these more ambitious applications has generally progressed more gradually than initial predictions suggested.

articles.title: Fibre-Optic Cable
articles.description: Sending data as pulses of light through glass threads.
articles.content:
Fibre-optic cable transmits data as pulses of light through extremely thin, flexible strands of glass or plastic, typically thinner than a human hair, allowing information to travel at close to the speed of light with very little loss of signal quality even over long distances.

The technology was developed through the 1960s and 1970s, with the physicist Charles Kao making key theoretical breakthroughs in 1966 that showed how impurities in glass, rather than the glass itself, were the main obstacle to practical long-distance fibre-optic communication, work for which he later received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009.

Today a vast global network of undersea and land-based fibre-optic cables forms the physical backbone of the internet, carrying the overwhelming majority of international data traffic, including phone calls, video streams and financial transactions, and the continued expansion of high-speed fibre connections to homes and businesses remains a major infrastructure priority for many countries.

articles.title: Satellite Internet
articles.description: Bringing broadband to remote places from orbit.
articles.content:
Satellite internet provides internet access using signals relayed through satellites orbiting the Earth, rather than through cables buried in the ground or strung on poles, making it particularly valuable for connecting remote, rural or otherwise hard-to-reach areas where laying traditional cable infrastructure would be prohibitively expensive or impractical.

Older satellite internet systems relied on a small number of satellites in high geostationary orbit, about 36,000 kilometres above the Earth, which resulted in a noticeable delay, or latency, in the signal because of the great distance the signal had to travel, making the service poorly suited to activities such as online gaming or video calls that depend on very fast response times.

Newer systems, most notably SpaceX's Starlink, launched from 2019 onward, use large constellations of thousands of much smaller satellites in low Earth orbit, only a few hundred kilometres up, considerably reducing latency and making satellite internet a genuinely practical option for a much wider range of everyday internet uses in areas previously underserved by traditional broadband.

articles.title: The Video Game Industry
articles.description: The business behind interactive entertainment.
articles.content:
The video game industry designs, develops, publishes and sells video games, and it has grown into one of the largest sectors of the global entertainment industry, generating more annual revenue than the film and music industries combined in many recent years.

The industry traces its commercial origins to early arcade games in the 1970s, such as Pong, and expanded significantly through home video game consoles in the 1980s and personal computer gaming, before the rise of mobile gaming on smartphones from the late 2000s dramatically broadened the audience for video games well beyond traditional dedicated gamers, reaching a truly mass global market.

Major games can now cost hundreds of millions of dollars to develop, comparable to or exceeding the budgets of major Hollywood films, and the industry has also given rise to significant related sectors, including competitive esports, live game streaming on platforms such as Twitch, and a large market for downloadable additional content and in-game purchases within otherwise free-to-play games.

articles.title: Video Game Consoles
articles.description: Dedicated devices built for playing games.
articles.content:
A video game console is a specialised computing device designed primarily for playing video games, typically connected to a television or other display, distinguishing it from general-purpose personal computers that can run games alongside many other kinds of software.

The Magnavox Odyssey, released in 1972, is generally credited as the first commercial home video game console, though the format only became a true cultural phenomenon following the release of the Atari 2600 in 1977, which popularised the use of interchangeable game cartridges. Nintendo's Entertainment System, launched in the mid-1980s, is widely credited with helping to revive the North American video game market after a significant industry downturn in the early 1980s.

Successive generations of consoles from companies including Nintendo, Sony, with its PlayStation line launched in 1994, and Microsoft, with its Xbox launched in 2001, have competed closely for decades, each generation typically bringing significant improvements in graphics quality, processing power and online connectivity for multiplayer gaming.

articles.title: Self-Driving Cars
articles.description: Vehicles designed to navigate without a human driver.
articles.content:
A self-driving car, also called an autonomous vehicle, is a vehicle capable of sensing its surrounding environment and navigating, to varying degrees, without requiring constant direct human input, using a combination of sensors such as cameras, radar and often lidar, alongside sophisticated software to interpret the surrounding environment and make driving decisions.

The technology is often described using a scale of driving automation levels, ranging from no automation at all up to full autonomy, in which a vehicle can handle all driving tasks under all conditions without ever requiring human intervention, a level of capability that remains an ongoing engineering and regulatory challenge rather than a fully achieved commercial reality as of the mid-2020s.

Companies including Waymo, a subsidiary of Google's parent company Alphabet, and Tesla have been at the forefront of developing and deploying self-driving technology, with Waymo operating limited commercial autonomous taxi services in several American cities, though widespread, fully unsupervised self-driving cars operating reliably in all conditions and locations remain a significant unsolved technical and regulatory challenge.

articles.title: The History of Telecommunications
articles.description: From telegraph wires to global networks.
articles.content:
Telecommunications, the transmission of information over distance, has transformed dramatically since the invention of the electric telegraph in the 1830s and 1840s, which for the first time allowed messages to be sent almost instantly over long distances using electrical signals sent through wires, replacing far slower methods such as physically carried letters or visual signal towers.

The telephone, patented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, allowed voice itself to be transmitted electrically, and telephone networks expanded steadily through the 20th century, eventually connecting most of the world. Radio, developed from the work of figures including Guglielmo Marconi in the 1890s, subsequently allowed wireless transmission of both signals and, eventually, audio broadcasts, reaching audiences without any physical wired connection at all.

The 20th century's later telecommunications developments, including satellites, fibre-optic cables and eventually mobile phone networks and the internet, progressively wove these earlier technologies together into the highly interconnected, largely wireless and near-instantaneous global communications infrastructure that much of the world now relies on daily.

articles.title: Radio Technology
articles.description: Wireless transmission using electromagnetic waves.
articles.content:
Radio technology transmits information wirelessly using electromagnetic waves, a discovery that grew from the theoretical work of the physicist James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s and the subsequent experimental demonstrations of radio waves by Heinrich Hertz in the late 1880s, work that Guglielmo Marconi then built upon to develop practical long-distance wireless communication systems from the 1890s onward.

Radio broadcasting, in which audio content is transmitted to a wide public audience rather than between two specific points, became a significant mass medium from the 1920s onward, and for several decades it remained the dominant means by which most people received news, entertainment and, particularly during major world events, real-time information, before television gradually became more dominant from the mid-20th century.

Beyond traditional broadcasting, radio technology underpins numerous other essential modern applications, including mobile phone networks, Wi-Fi, GPS satellite navigation and air traffic control communications, making the broader principle of transmitting information via electromagnetic waves one of the most foundational and pervasive technologies in modern life.

articles.title: The Computer Mouse
articles.description: The pointing device that made computers easier to use.
articles.content:
The computer mouse is a handheld pointing device that allows a user to control a cursor on a computer screen by physically moving the device across a flat surface, translating that physical movement into corresponding on-screen movement, a considerably more intuitive method of interacting with graphical interfaces than typing text-based commands alone.

The device was invented by the American engineer Douglas Engelbart in 1964, and it was publicly demonstrated to considerable acclaim in a landmark 1968 presentation now often referred to as the Mother of All Demos, which also showcased several other now-fundamental computing concepts considerably ahead of their time, including hypertext links and video conferencing.

The mouse remained a relatively niche, specialised device for over a decade until it was adopted commercially by Xerox and, considerably more influentially, by Apple with its Macintosh computer in 1984, which helped establish the mouse as a standard input device for personal computers for decades afterward, alongside the graphical user interfaces it was specifically designed to help navigate.

articles.title: The Computer Keyboard
articles.description: The primary way we type into computers.
articles.content:
A computer keyboard is an input device consisting of an arrangement of keys, used to enter letters, numbers, symbols and commands into a computer. Its layout descends directly from mechanical typewriters, which were developed and gradually refined throughout the 19th century, well before the invention of electronic computers themselves.

The QWERTY layout, named for the first six letters appearing on its top row of letter keys, was patented in 1878 and became the dominant standard keyboard layout across much of the world, despite the later development of alternative layouts, such as the Dvorak layout designed in the 1930s, that some studies suggest may allow somewhat faster typing for many users, though QWERTY's deep entrenchment has made it extremely difficult to displace in practice.

Modern keyboards include additional function keys not found on mechanical typewriters, and specialised variants exist for different needs, including compact keyboards designed for laptops, ergonomic keyboards designed to reduce strain during extended typing, and on-screen virtual keyboards that have become standard on touchscreen smartphones and tablets.

articles.title: USB
articles.description: The universal connector for computer devices.
articles.content:
USB, or Universal Serial Bus, is a widely adopted standard for connecting a vast range of peripheral devices to computers and other electronic devices, including keyboards, mice, external storage drives, printers and phone chargers, and it was specifically developed to replace the confusing variety of different, often incompatible connector types that had previously existed for different kinds of devices.

The standard was developed collaboratively by a group of major technology companies and first released in 1996, though widespread adoption took several more years as manufacturers gradually transitioned away from older connector types. Successive versions of the USB standard have delivered substantial improvements in data transfer speed and the amount of electrical power the connection can deliver, allowing USB to be used not just for data transfer but increasingly for charging devices as well.

The USB-C connector, introduced in 2014, uses a symmetrical, reversible design that can be inserted either way up, addressing a long-standing minor but widely shared source of everyday user frustration with earlier USB connector designs, and it has since been increasingly adopted as a common charging standard across many different device types and manufacturers.

articles.title: Hard Drives and Storage
articles.description: How computers keep data long-term.
articles.content:
A hard disk drive is a data storage device that stores digital information magnetically on one or more rapidly spinning circular disks, called platters, allowing a computer to retain files and programs even after it is switched off, unlike a computer's much faster but temporary working memory, or RAM, which loses its contents when power is removed.

IBM introduced the first commercial hard disk drive in 1956, a machine roughly the size of two large refrigerators that could store only about five megabytes of data, an almost unimaginably tiny amount by today's standards, illustrating just how dramatically storage capacity has increased relative to physical size and cost over the subsequent decades of continuous technological development.

Solid-state drives, which store data using flash memory chips rather than any spinning mechanical parts at all, have become increasingly dominant in many devices since the 2010s, offering considerably faster data access speeds, improved reliability due to having no moving parts to wear out or fail mechanically, and lower power consumption, though traditional mechanical hard drives generally remain more cost-effective for very large-scale bulk data storage needs.

articles.title: RAM
articles.description: The fast, temporary memory computers use while working.
articles.content:
RAM, or random-access memory, is a type of computer memory used to temporarily store data that a computer's processor is actively working with, allowing extremely fast access to that data compared with a computer's slower, longer-term storage such as a hard drive or solid-state drive.

Unlike long-term storage, RAM is volatile, meaning that its entire contents are lost whenever the computer loses power, which is why any unsaved work in an open document or application is typically lost if a computer crashes or is suddenly switched off before the user has an opportunity to save their progress to permanent storage.

The amount of RAM a device has significantly affects how many programs it can run smoothly at the same time and how quickly it can switch between different open tasks, and RAM capacity in consumer devices has grown enormously over recent decades, from early personal computers that operated with only a few kilobytes of memory to modern computers and smartphones that commonly include many gigabytes.

articles.title: Graphics Cards
articles.description: Specialised hardware for rendering images and video.
articles.content:
A graphics card, built around a specialised processor called a graphics processing unit or GPU, is dedicated hardware designed specifically to rapidly render the images, video and visual effects displayed on a computer screen, a highly demanding, specialised computational task that a computer's general-purpose main processor alone would typically struggle to handle efficiently at the speed required for smooth visuals.

GPUs are particularly well suited to performing very large numbers of simple mathematical calculations simultaneously in parallel, an architectural strength that originally made them especially valuable for rendering the complex, fast-changing three-dimensional graphics found in modern video games, an application that drove much of the early consumer demand for increasingly powerful dedicated graphics cards.

More recently, this same underlying parallel processing capability has proven unexpectedly valuable well beyond graphics rendering, particularly for training the large neural networks used in modern artificial intelligence systems, a development that has driven enormous additional demand for high-performance GPUs from AI researchers and companies, and has correspondingly made GPU manufacturers such as Nvidia significantly more prominent and valuable within the broader technology industry.

articles.title: Supercomputers
articles.description: The world's most powerful computing machines.
articles.content:
A supercomputer is a computer system with extremely high computational performance compared with typical general-purpose computers, generally built by combining vast numbers of individual processors working together in parallel to tackle enormously complex calculations that would take ordinary computers an impractically long time to complete.

Supercomputers are typically used for highly demanding scientific and engineering applications, including detailed climate and weather modelling, simulating nuclear weapons safety without the need for actual physical explosive testing, and, increasingly in recent years, training some of the largest and most powerful artificial intelligence models, which require enormous computational resources over often quite lengthy and expensive training periods.

The world's fastest supercomputers are formally ranked twice a year in a widely followed public list called the TOP500, and the sustained race among different countries and research institutions to build ever more powerful systems has become both a matter of considerable scientific achievement and, at times, of significant national technological prestige and competition between major world powers.

articles.title: Servers
articles.description: The computers that power websites and online services.
articles.content:
A server is a computer, or often specialised software running on a computer, that provides services, resources or data to other computers, known as clients, typically over a network such as the internet. When you visit a website, for example, your device acts as a client requesting and receiving data from a remote web server that stores and delivers the actual website content.

Unlike typical personal computers used directly by an individual, servers are generally designed and specifically optimised for reliability, security and the ability to efficiently handle many simultaneous requests from potentially large numbers of different users at once, and they are commonly housed in specialised, climate-controlled data centres specifically designed to keep them running continuously.

Modern servers increasingly run as virtual machines within cloud computing environments, allowing computing resources to be flexibly allocated, shared and scaled dynamically across many different customers and varying levels of demand, an approach that has made deploying and running internet services considerably more efficient and accessible than the earlier era of businesses needing to individually own and directly maintain their own dedicated physical server hardware.

articles.title: Domain Names
articles.description: The addresses that make the internet navigable.
articles.content:
A domain name is a human-readable address, such as example.com, used to identify a particular website or other resource on the internet, considerably easier for people to remember and type than the underlying numerical IP addresses that computers actually use to locate and communicate directly with each other across the network.

The domain name system, which translates these human-friendly names into the numerical addresses computers require, was developed in 1983 by the computer scientist Paul Mockapetris, replacing an earlier, considerably less scalable system that had relied on manually maintaining and distributing a single shared master list of all known network names and addresses across the entire early internet.

Domain names are organised hierarchically, with top-level domains such as .com, .org and country-specific codes such as .az for Azerbaijan sitting at the top of the structure, and the registration and ongoing management of domain names worldwide is coordinated by an international non-profit organisation called ICANN, established in 1998 specifically to help oversee this critical shared internet infrastructure.

articles.title: Web Browsers
articles.description: The software we use to view websites.
articles.content:
A web browser is software used to access, display and navigate websites and other content on the World Wide Web, translating the underlying code of a web page into the visually formatted text, images and interactive elements that users actually see and interact with on their screen.

Mosaic, released in 1993, was among the first web browsers to become widely popular, notably for its ability to display images directly alongside text within the same page, a significant improvement over the largely text-only browsers that had preceded it. The subsequent so-called browser wars of the 1990s, primarily fought between Netscape Navigator and Microsoft's Internet Explorer, considerably shaped the web's early technical development, sometimes for better and sometimes for worse in terms of maintaining consistent standards across different browsers.

Google's Chrome browser, launched in 2008, has since become the dominant browser used worldwide, and it is built on an open-source software project called Chromium, which several other major competing browsers, including Microsoft's modern version of Edge, have also since adopted as their own underlying technical foundation.

articles.title: HTML and CSS
articles.description: The languages that build the visual web.
articles.content:
HTML, HyperText Markup Language, is the standard language used to structure and describe the content of web pages, defining fundamental elements such as headings, paragraphs, images and links, while CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, is a separate, closely related language used to control the specific visual presentation and layout of that HTML content, including colours, fonts and precise page positioning.

HTML was created by Tim Berners-Lee alongside the World Wide Web itself in 1989 and 1990, while CSS was subsequently proposed a few years later, in 1994, specifically to separate a web page's underlying content and structure from decisions about how that content should actually look when displayed, an important and influential separation of concerns that made building and, crucially, maintaining large, consistent websites considerably more practical and manageable.

Both languages have continued to evolve considerably since their creation, with the current widely used version, HTML5, released in 2014, adding substantial native support for multimedia content such as video and audio directly within the browser, reducing the earlier reliance on separate third-party plugins such as Adobe Flash to display such content on web pages.

articles.title: The App Store Economy
articles.description: How mobile apps became a major industry.
articles.content:
The app store economy refers to the substantial business ecosystem that has developed around digital marketplaces, most significantly Apple's App Store and Google Play, where mobile apps are distributed to smartphone and tablet users, generating very substantial revenue both for the platform operators and for the many individual app developers who sell their software or, more commonly, offer in-app purchases and advertising within otherwise free apps.

App stores typically operate by charging developers a commission, commonly around 15 to 30 percent depending on specific circumstances and developer size, on paid app sales and in-app purchases made through the platform's own payment system, an arrangement that has drawn considerable and growing scrutiny from developers, competition regulators and courts in multiple countries in recent years.

Major ongoing legal and regulatory disputes, including a prominent case brought by the game developer Epic Games against both Apple and Google beginning in 2020, have specifically challenged the fairness of these established app store commission structures and, more broadly, the platform operators' tight overall control over what apps can be distributed and how, reflecting wider public and regulatory debate about competition in digital markets.

articles.title: Net Neutrality
articles.description: The principle that internet providers should treat all traffic equally.
articles.content:
Net neutrality is the principle that internet service providers should treat all data travelling across their networks equally, without deliberately blocking, deliberately slowing down, or charging differently for access to different websites, applications or types of online content based on their own commercial interests or agreements.

Supporters of net neutrality argue that it is essential for maintaining a genuinely fair and open internet, preventing large internet service providers from favouring their own affiliated services or from charging other companies extra fees for reliably fast access to consumers, which could otherwise potentially disadvantage smaller businesses, startups and independent websites that cannot afford to pay such additional fees.

The issue has proven particularly contentious as a matter of policy in the United States, where formal net neutrality regulations have been repeatedly introduced, subsequently repealed, and then reconsidered again by regulators across successive changes in political administration since the mid-2010s, while numerous other countries around the world have adopted their own distinct approaches and regulatory frameworks to the underlying question.

articles.title: The Digital Divide
articles.description: Unequal access to technology and the internet.
articles.content:
The digital divide refers to the significant gap between individuals, communities or entire countries that have convenient, affordable access to modern digital technology, particularly reliable internet access, and those that do not, a gap with real and often substantial consequences for education, employment opportunities and access to essential information and services.

The divide exists along multiple overlapping dimensions, including significant differences between urban and rural areas, where laying the necessary physical infrastructure can be considerably more difficult and expensive, between wealthier and poorer households, who may struggle to afford the cost of devices or ongoing internet subscriptions, and between richer and poorer countries more broadly, with internet access still considerably less common across much of the developing world.

The COVID-19 pandemic, beginning in 2020, drew considerable renewed public and policy attention to the digital divide's real-world consequences, as widespread school closures and a broad shift to remote work highlighted just how significantly a lack of reliable home internet access and suitable devices could disadvantage particular students and workers, prompting many governments to expand efforts specifically aimed at increasing affordable broadband access.

articles.title: Online Privacy
articles.description: Protecting personal information in the digital age.
articles.content:
Online privacy refers to the ability of individuals to control what personal information about themselves is collected, stored, shared and used by the websites, apps and online services they interact with, an area of growing public and regulatory concern as an increasing proportion of daily life has moved online.

Many websites and apps collect considerable amounts of user data, including detailed browsing habits, precise location information and personal preferences, often used to build detailed profiles for the purposes of targeted advertising or to improve and personalise the service being offered, a business model that has driven much of the modern internet's largely advertising-funded economy but has also raised significant, ongoing ethical and legal concerns about the scope and appropriate limits of such data collection.

The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in 2018, established some of the world's most influential and comprehensive privacy protections, giving individuals significant new legal rights over how their personal data can be collected and used by companies, and it has since prompted many other countries and jurisdictions around the world to introduce broadly similar privacy legislation of their own.

articles.title: Biometrics
articles.description: Using the body itself to verify identity.
articles.content:
Biometrics refers to technology that identifies or verifies a person's identity based on unique physical or behavioural characteristics of their own body, such as fingerprints, facial features, iris patterns or, in some more advanced systems, even a person's distinctive way of walking or typing.

Fingerprint recognition has a particularly long history in security and forensic applications, dating back well over a century, but biometric technology became genuinely mainstream in everyday consumer devices following Apple's introduction of fingerprint-based Touch ID in 2013, and subsequently facial recognition-based Face ID in 2017, both offering a considerably faster and often more secure everyday alternative to typing a traditional password to unlock a personal device.

While biometric authentication offers notable everyday convenience, since a fingerprint or face genuinely cannot be easily forgotten in the way a password can, it has also raised significant privacy concerns, since biometric data is inherently permanent and cannot be changed if compromised in the way a stolen password can simply be reset, and various governments have introduced differing specific regulations governing precisely how biometric data may be collected, stored and used by companies.

articles.title: Smart Home Technology
articles.description: Connected devices that automate the household.
articles.content:
Smart home technology refers to internet-connected devices within a household that can be remotely monitored and controlled, often automated according to schedules or specific triggering conditions, or voice-activated through devices such as smart speakers, encompassing products ranging from smart thermostats and connected lighting to security cameras and automated door locks.

The category expanded very substantially in consumer popularity from around the mid-2010s onward, driven significantly by the introduction of affordable voice-controlled smart speakers, including Amazon's Echo, launched in 2014 with its Alexa voice assistant, which provided users with a simple, convenient central way to control multiple different connected smart home devices using natural spoken commands rather than separate individual apps.

A persistent significant challenge for the smart home industry has been the historical lack of a single common technical standard, meaning that devices from different manufacturers have often failed to work smoothly and reliably together, though industry-wide efforts such as the Matter standard, introduced in 2022 by a broad coalition of major technology companies, aim to significantly improve compatibility and interoperability between devices from different manufacturers going forward.

articles.title: The Internet of Things
articles.description: Everyday objects connected to the internet.
articles.content:
The internet of things, often abbreviated as IoT, refers to the broad and rapidly growing network of everyday physical objects, well beyond traditional computers and smartphones, that are now embedded with sensors, software and internet connectivity, allowing them to collect and exchange useful data over the internet, ranging from smart home devices and wearable fitness trackers to industrial sensors monitoring factory equipment.

The specific term was coined in 1999 by the British technology pioneer Kevin Ashton, originally in the more specific context of connecting supply chain tracking sensors to the internet, though the underlying broader concept has since expanded enormously to cover an extremely wide and growing range of connected devices used across many different industries and everyday consumer contexts.

Industrial applications of IoT technology, sometimes referred to specifically as the industrial internet of things, have become particularly significant and valuable, since networked sensors embedded throughout factories, agricultural operations and city infrastructure can help detect equipment problems considerably earlier, optimise resource use more efficiently, and improve overall operational efficiency, though the rapidly growing number of connected devices has also correspondingly raised significant new cybersecurity concerns and challenges for organisations to manage.

articles.title: Battery Technology
articles.description: The chemistry that powers portable devices.
articles.content:
Battery technology stores electrical energy chemically so that it can later be released on demand to power portable devices, from smartphones and laptops to electric vehicles, and steady, substantial improvements in battery technology over recent decades have been a genuinely critical enabling factor behind much of the growth of modern portable and wireless electronics.

Lithium-ion batteries, first commercially introduced by the Japanese company Sony in 1991, transformed portable electronics by offering considerably higher energy density, meaning more stored energy for a given battery weight and size, than the older nickel-cadmium batteries that had been the previous standard, and lithium-ion technology remains the dominant, most widely used rechargeable battery technology across most modern portable devices and electric vehicles today.

Ongoing battery research continues to focus intensively on further improving energy density to extend device runtime and vehicle range, reducing battery charging times, extending overall battery lifespan through many repeated charge cycles, and developing safer, potentially more sustainable alternative battery chemistries, since batteries have become an increasingly critical bottleneck technology for the continued broader transition toward renewable energy storage and widespread electric vehicle adoption worldwide.

articles.title: Touchscreens
articles.description: Displays that respond directly to touch.
articles.content:
A touchscreen is a display that can detect and respond directly to the touch of a finger or a stylus, allowing users to interact directly and intuitively with what is shown on the screen itself, without necessarily needing a separate physical input device such as a keyboard or mouse to control the interface.

Early experimental touchscreen technology dates back to the 1960s and 1970s, but touchscreens remained a relatively niche, specialised technology, used mainly in specific applications such as public information kiosks and certain industrial equipment, for several subsequent decades before becoming genuinely mainstream. Apple's iPhone, launched in 2007, was particularly influential in popularising a specific type of touchscreen, called capacitive touch, which could accurately detect multiple simultaneous finger touches at once, enabling now-familiar gestures such as pinching to zoom in or out on an image.

Touchscreens have since become the dominant standard input method for smartphones and tablets, and they are increasingly common in numerous other everyday contexts as well, including laptop computers, car dashboards, home appliances and public self-service kiosks, reflecting a broader ongoing shift toward more direct, intuitive physical interaction with digital interfaces across many different device types.

articles.title: Laptop Computers
articles.description: Portable personal computers.
articles.content:
A laptop computer is a portable personal computer designed to be small and light enough to be easily carried and comfortably used on one's lap or on a small table or desk, combining the display, keyboard, processing hardware and, crucially, a rechargeable battery all together within a single compact, foldable unit.

Early portable computers in the late 1970s and early 1980s, sometimes described at the time as luggable computers, were still quite heavy and bulky by modern standards, often weighing well over ten kilograms, but the format gradually became considerably lighter, more compact and more genuinely portable through the 1980s and 1990s as component miniaturisation, battery technology and overall engineering design steadily improved.

Laptops have become increasingly dominant relative to traditional desktop computers for many typical personal and even much professional computing use, particularly as their processing performance has increasingly closed the earlier significant performance gap with desktop machines, and the growing popularity of remote and hybrid work arrangements in recent years has further reinforced the practical everyday value of a genuinely portable, all-in-one personal computing device.

articles.title: Azerbaijan's Technology Sector
articles.description: The country's growing digital economy.
articles.content:
Azerbaijan has been working to develop its information technology sector as part of a broader effort to diversify its economy beyond oil and gas, its traditional main source of national income for over a century. A key initiative has been the establishment of ASAN xidmet, launched in 2012, a widely praised e-government service that consolidates numerous different public services into unified physical service centres and an accompanying online platform, considerably simplifying many everyday bureaucratic processes for citizens.

The country has also invested in dedicated technology infrastructure, including the High Technologies Park established near Baku, intended specifically to support and encourage the growth of local software development and technology companies through various tax incentives and other forms of government support, as part of a broader strategic goal of building a more diversified, less oil-dependent national economy over the coming decades.

Azerbaijan's own satellite operator, Azercosmos, established in 2010, and the country's steadily growing base of local software developers and increasingly active technology startups, reflect this ongoing effort to build domestic technical capacity and expertise, even as the country continues working to expand reliable, affordable broadband internet access more evenly across both its urban centres and more rural regions.

articles.title: Voice Assistants
articles.description: AI helpers that respond to spoken commands.
articles.content:
A voice assistant is a software application that uses speech recognition and natural language processing to understand spoken commands and questions, and responds either verbally or by carrying out a requested action, such as setting a timer, playing music or answering a factual question.

Apple's Siri, introduced in 2011, was among the first voice assistants to reach a truly mass consumer audience through its integration into the iPhone, and it was followed by competitors including Amazon's Alexa in 2014, closely tied to its Echo smart speaker line, and Google Assistant in 2016, each aiming to become a central, convenient way for users to interact with their devices and, increasingly, their connected smart home devices using natural spoken language.

More recent advances in large language models have considerably improved voice assistants' ability to handle more open-ended, conversational questions rather than only a fixed, narrower set of pre-programmed commands, and voice assistants have become an increasingly common everyday presence in homes, cars and on smartphones worldwide, though concerns about the privacy implications of always-listening microphones in the home have remained a persistent subject of public discussion.

articles.title: E-books
articles.description: Digital books read on screens.
articles.content:
An e-book, or electronic book, is a digital publication designed to be read on a computer, tablet, smartphone or a specialised dedicated e-reader device, rather than printed on physical paper, and typically stored and distributed in specific digital file formats designed for text that can automatically reflow and adjust to fit different screen sizes.

While experimental digital text formats existed earlier, the e-book market only became genuinely mainstream following the launch of Amazon's dedicated Kindle e-reader device in 2007, which combined a large catalogue of available digital titles with a specialised display technology called electronic ink, designed specifically to closely mimic the appearance of ordinary printed paper and to be considerably easier on the eyes than a typical backlit screen during extended reading sessions.

E-books offer several notable practical advantages over printed books, including the ability to instantly download new titles without needing to visit a physical shop, to adjust text size for easier reading, and to carry an entire personal library's worth of books within a single lightweight portable device, though many readers continue to also strongly value printed physical books, and both formats have generally continued to coexist rather than one fully displacing the other.

articles.title: Podcasting
articles.description: On-demand audio shows delivered over the internet.
articles.content:
A podcast is a series of digital audio, and sometimes video, episodes made available for people to download or stream on demand over the internet, typically focused around a particular ongoing theme, topic or format, and generally released as part of a continuing series that listeners can subscribe to and follow.

The term podcast itself, a blend of iPod and broadcast, was coined in 2004, not long after Apple's portable iPod music player had become hugely popular, though the underlying technology allowing audio files to be automatically and conveniently delivered to a personal device as new episodes became available had been developed slightly earlier by other technologists.

Podcasting experienced particularly significant, sustained growth in popularity from the mid-2010s onward, considerably aided by the near-universal availability of smartphones and reliable, plentiful mobile internet data, and major platforms including Spotify have subsequently invested very heavily in podcast content and exclusive licensing deals, helping firmly establish podcasting as a genuinely significant and influential part of the broader modern media and entertainment landscape.

articles.title: Chatbots
articles.description: Software designed to hold conversations with people.
articles.content:
A chatbot is a software program specifically designed to simulate and conduct conversation with human users, typically through either typed text or, increasingly, spoken voice interaction, ranging from relatively simple rule-based systems that can only recognise and respond to a limited, predefined set of specific keywords and phrases, to considerably more sophisticated modern systems built on advanced artificial intelligence.

Early chatbots, such as the influential ELIZA program created in 1966, which simulated a psychotherapist by cleverly rephrasing a user's own statements back to them as follow-up questions, relied on comparatively simple pattern-matching rules rather than any genuine underlying understanding of language or meaning, yet still managed to convince some early users they were having a surprisingly natural and meaningful conversation.

The public release of considerably more advanced chatbots built on large language models from 2022 onward marked a dramatic and widely noted leap forward in chatbot capability, since these newer systems can hold genuinely open-ended, remarkably fluent conversations, answer a very wide range of factual and creative questions, and assist with substantial writing and other cognitive tasks, though they can also sometimes confidently produce inaccurate or entirely fabricated information, an ongoing limitation of the technology that developers continue actively working to address.
